description: 80% hydration sourdough is a wet dough with big holes and a custardy crumb. Work out the water, starter, and salt for any flour weight, with the table.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 350 g water, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. Total dough 910 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Total water is 80% of the flour: 500 × 0.80 = 400 g. Water to add is 400 - 50 = 350 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.

faqs.answer: High-protein bread flour, around 12.5% protein or more. The gluten network has to hold a lot of water, and weaker flour will let the dough spread instead of rising. Whole wheat and freshly milled flour absorb more water, so they can handle 80% well, but they also ferment faster.
faqs.question: What flour can handle 80% hydration?

faqs.answer: Because the starter already brings water. For 500 g of flour, 80% hydration means 400 g of water in total, and 100 g of starter brings 50 g of that water. You add the remaining 350 g. Adding all 400 g on top of the starter would push the true hydration to about 82%.
faqs.question: Why is the water to add only 350 g and not 400 g?

felicityNote: Eighty percent humbled me the first time. The dough looked like soup, and then the folds worked and it baked into the best loaf I had made that year.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 80%, every 100 g of flour holds 80 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add, holding back about 30 g of the water for now. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left. The dough will be very soft and sticky. Add the held-back water only if the dough feels like it can take it.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then fold every 30 minutes for the first two to three hours: stretch and folds early, coil folds once the dough is full of air. Use wet hands throughout.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, domed, and jiggly. Shape gently with a bench scraper, keeping the air in. Do not try to force a tight shape the way you would with a firm dough.

howToSteps.name: Cold proof, then bake
howToSteps.text: Basket the loaf seam side up, cover, and refrigerate overnight. Bake straight from the fridge in a hot Dutch oven. The cold dough scores cleanly and springs well.

lede: At 80% hydration the dough is wet, slack, and full of promise: big holes, a custardy crumb, and a loaf that eats like a bakery country bread. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter, so the hydration you ask for is the hydration you get.

name: 80% Hydration
summary: 500 g flour at 80% hydration: add 450 g flour, 350 g water, 100 g starter, 10 g salt.
title: Sourdough Calculator: 80% Hydration
tutorial: Eighty percent is wet dough, properly wet. When you first mix it, the dough will look more like a thick batter than a bread dough, and your first thought will be that you measured wrong. You did not. This is what 80% feels like, and the folds are what turn it into bread.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 500 g of total flour at 80% hydration, the dough holds 400 g of water in total. Your starter brings 50 g of that water, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 350 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g.

Flour is not optional at this hydration. You want bread flour with around 12.5% protein or more, because the gluten network has to hold all that water and still stand up in the oven. Weaker flour will give you a dough that spreads instead of rising, and no amount of folding fixes a flour that cannot take the water. Whole wheat and freshly milled flour absorb more water than white flour, so they can handle 80% well, but they also ferment faster, so watch the clock.

The technique that makes 80% work is the coil fold. Later in bulk fermentation, when the dough is full of air, stretching tears it. A coil fold lifts the dough from the middle with both hands and lets the ends fold under, which builds strength without knocking the gas out. Alternate stretch and folds early with coil folds late, every 30 minutes, and the dough will tighten up in a way that surprises you every time.

Shaping an 80% dough is a light touch. A bench scraper, a wet surface or a light dusting of flour, and quick moves. Do not try to force the tight ball you would make with a 65% dough; this dough wants a gentle envelope fold and a basket to hold it. Cold-proof it overnight in the fridge, and bake it straight from cold. The fridge firms the dough, the score stays open, and the oven spring does the rest.
